'''Aequian''' is an extinct Italic language presumed spoken by the people the Romans termed [[Aequi]] and Aequicoli living in the [[Alban Hills]] of northeast [[Latium]] and the central [[Apennines]] east of them during the early and middle [[Roman Republic]]; that is, approximately from the 5th to the 3rd century BC, when they were defeated by the armies of Rome and were subsequently Romanized. As the area was heavily colonized by Latin speakers from Rome, most of the inscriptions from there are in Latin. Two undated inscriptions appear to be in a different dialect, termed Aequian by the scholars with the presumption that in fact they represent the language of the entire pre-Roman tribe. Not enough text survives to deduce any more than that it belonged to the [[Italic languages|Italic]] branch of the [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] language family.{{Citation needed|date=November 2023}}

==Corpus==
Aequian is scantily documented by two inscriptions. Conway's publication of Italic inscriptions adds a gloss, several place names and several dozen personal names, but it does not distinguish which of these are certainly [[endonym]]s and which are Latin [[exonym]]s in use by the Latin-speaking population.<ref name=Conway>{{cite book |first=Robert Seymour |last=Conway |title=The Italic Dialects |url=https://archive.org/details/italicdialects02conw | year=1897 |location=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=301–305}}</ref> It is possible that they would have been the same in both cases, but such a hypothesis remains unproven.

The Inscription of [[Alba Fucens]] is a bronze plate inscribed with {{lang|xae|ALBSI PATRE}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Ernout|1916|pp=43–44}} gives the CIL number, as the inscription was originally taken to be early Latin: [[Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum|CIL]] I<sup>2</sup> 385, VI 3672, IX 4177.</ref> Conway reconstructs the first word as {{lang|xae|*albe(n)si}}, a [[dative case]]. [[Philip Baldi|Baldi]] translates the text into Latin as {{lang|la|Albano patri}}, two datives, and into English as "To the (god named) Alban Father."<ref>{{cite book |first=Philip |last=Baldi |author-link=Philip Baldi|title=The Foundations of Latin |location=Berlin |publisher=Mouton de Gruyter |year=2002 |series=Trends in Linguistics: Studies and Monographs | page=122}}</ref>

The second document is the Inscription of Cliternia (Capradosso) in [[Petrella Salto]], an inscribed stone in a spring dissociated from context by nature (it rolled down a hill).<ref>[[Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum|CIL]] IX, 4171, according to {{harvnb|Ernout|1916|p=45}}.</ref> The text is:<ref name=Conway/>
: {{lang|xae|VIA INFERIOR {{!}} PRIVATAST {{!}} T VMBRENI C F {{!}}}}
: {{lang|xae|PRECARIO {{!}} ITVR {{!}} PECVS PLOSTRV {{!}} NIQVIS AGAT}}

which is a notice stating that the road is private, passage by permission of Titus Umbrenus, son of Gaius, but beasts of burden are forbidden.
